# forbes-brewster-openai-warrant-2025-10-20
- **URL:** https://cdn.lawreportgroup.com/acuris/files/Law-Report-Group-Files-New/AI%20Warrants%20Pt%201%20Forbes%20article.pdf (Law Report Group reprint PDF of the Forbes article; forbes.com itself returns 403) · **Accessed:** 2026-09-16 · **For:** v2→v3 response round, slice L
- **What it establishes:** Thomas Brewster, Forbes, "DHS Ordered OpenAI To Share User Data In First Known Warrant For ChatGPT Prompts" (published Oct 20, 2025, 09:12am EDT; updated 04:34pm EDT), full text read (5 pp.). Brewster reviewed the warrant after it was unsealed in Maine. HSI had been chatting undercover with the admin of a dark-web CSAM site, who volunteered two ChatGPT exchanges (Sherlock Holmes/Q; a Trump-style Y.M.C.A. poem). The warrant ordered OpenAI to provide information on the person who entered the prompts (other conversations, names, addresses, payment data). Forbes states flatly that the government did NOT need OpenAI's data to identify the man: he was identified from biographical details given in undercover chats (health assessments, seven years in Germany, father served in Afghanistan) plus information from the military (worked at Ramstein; applied for DoD work). Named defendant: Drew Hoehner, 36. OpenAI's return was one Excel spreadsheet; Forbes says its contents are unknown and it might be used to corroborate the identification. Forbes does NOT date the identification relative to OpenAI's return.
- **Key passages:**
  - p. 2: "In the first known federal search warrant asking OpenAI for user data, reviewed by Forbes after it was unsealed in Maine last week, Homeland Security Investigations revealed it had been chatting with the administrator in an undercover capacity on the child exploitation site when the suspect noted they’d been using ChatGPT."
  - p. 3: "The government ordered OpenAI to provide various kinds of information on the person who entered the prompts, including details of other conversations they’d had with ChatGPT, names and addresses associated with the relevant accounts, as well as any payment data."
  - p. 3: "That makes this the first public example of this kind of reverse AI prompt request."
  - pp. 3–4: "However, the government did not require the OpenAI data to identify their man. Instead, they were able to glean enough information during undercover chats with the suspect to discover that he was connected to the U.S. military. The suspect disclosed, for instance, that he was going through health assessments, had lived in Germany for seven years and that his father had served in Afghanistan. They later learned from the military the suspect had worked on Ramstein Air Force Base in Germany and had applied for further work with the Department of Defense ..."
  - p. 5: "It’s unclear what specific data the government received. A document showed the search had been completed and OpenAI had provided agents with one Excel spreadsheet of information. ... It’s possible the information from OpenAI could be used to help prosecutors corroborate their identification of the defendant."
  - p. 5 (EFF's Jennifer Lynch, paraphrased by Forbes): the warrant "appeared limited in terms of focusing on two prompts from one user"; quoted: "That means it’s more important than ever for OpenAI and other AI companies to think about how to limit the amount of data they collect on their users".
- **Reliability:** Secondary but first-hand: the reporter read the unsealed court file. Reprint PDF is a faithful page capture of the Forbes page (byline, timestamps). The sentence that the OpenAI data was not required is Forbes's characterization; the court documents I read (see hoehner-openai-warrant-affidavit-and-return) neither confirm nor deny it.
- **Relevance to this project:** L1. Contradicts the essay's "identified a suspect ... from the content of two prompts" / "found a man from two prompts". Safe wording: "the first known federal search warrant asking OpenAI for user data" (Forbes's words); the warrant SOUGHT to identify a user from two prompts; agents identified him by other means.
